item.title: ONVIF vs GB/T 28181: How They Work Inside — Plug-and-Play Devices vs System-Level Networking
item.description: After MiBeeNvr v0.9 shipped ONVIF auto-discovery, manual camera configuration was mostly gone. The next question was whether to add GB/T 28181 uplink support, so I dug through the mechanics of both protocols. Most comparison articles online stop at “ONVIF is the international standard, GB28181 is the Chinese national standard”—which carries zero information for someone writing code. This post breaks both protocols down to the signaling-flow and message level: how ONVIF discovers devices and obtains stream URIs; how GB28181’s 20-digit codes address everything, how INVITE negotiates a stream, and what PS encapsulation actually is.

item.title: The Surveillance Protocol Panorama: A Four-Layer Map from Access to Compliance — What Each Protocol Is and When to Use It
item.description: The previous post took ONVIF and GB/T 28181 apart down to signaling and messages. But building an NVR means the protocol environment extends well beyond those two: vendor-private APIs on the camera side, a view-library standard on the public-security side, Ministry-of-Transport standards for vehicles, WebRTC for browser viewing, HLS for public distribution, and a national-crypto compliance stack. This post lays out the entire landscape—each protocol gets four sections: what it is → key technical points → its relationship with other protocols → its value to an NVR. Beginners can read it as an index; veterans can jump straight to the priority table.

item.title: Dual-Stack Cameras in the Field: What Happens When ONVIF and GB28181 Run Together, and Whether GB28181 Travels
item.description:
The first two posts covered protocol mechanics and the landscape; this one returns to device-side questions an NVR builder actually meets: can a camera hang both protocol stacks at once? With both enabled, what does it cost the camera, and what does it mean for an NVR that discovers cameras via ONVIF? Finally, a product question—does GB28181 actually get used overseas, and is it worth building for international markets?

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.10.1 → v0.11.0: fnOS Install Fixes + GB/T 28181 Support + Full-Day Playback Timeline
item.description: A few days after v0.10.0 went stable, fnOS users’ feedback boiled down to one sentence: it won’t install. It took seven rounds of installs on a live RK3582 fnOS box, plus SSH-ing into containers to read logs, to dig the three blockers out one by one. The previous release post here was still on v0.10.0-preview.1; that’s three versions unaccounted for — stable, patch, and now v0.11.0 — so this post covers them together.

item.title: The Rust and Go Ecosystems for ONVIF/GB28181: Library Selection, Source Reading, and a Hardware-Free Integration Path
item.description: The first three posts settled the protocol mechanics, the landscape, and the device side; the final question is concrete: which libraries to write it with. This survey went through everything usable in both ecosystems. The one-sentence verdict: ONVIF has workable libraries on both sides; the mature GB28181 implementations live on the Go/Java/C++ side while Rust’s are still young; and for streaming infrastructure (repackaging, distribution, egress) the Go ecosystem is clearly thicker.
